strengths: VisuRiddles fills a genuine gap: existing AVR benchmarks (RAVEN, PGM, ConceptARC) are synthetic and narrow, while real exam-based riddles with per-category perceptual/reasoning annotation are scarce. The five-dimension taxonomy grounded in cognitive science is well motivated.

The central finding—that fine-grained perception, not reasoning capacity, is the primary bottleneck—is well supported by multiple lines of evidence: (i) near-random performance of 17 models including thinking-mode/CoT variants, (ii) large accuracy jumps when perceptual descriptions replace raw images (Tab. 4, e.g., Sudoku 0→65 for Qwen2.5VL-72B), and (iii) qualitative case studies (Fig. 4).

The PRS framework's idea of pairing rendered riddles with structured, machine-generated perceptual annotations is practical and scalable, sidestepping expensive expert annotation of intermediate reasoning traces.
Broad evaluation coverage (11 open-source + 6 proprietary models, CoT and thinking variants) with reasonably detailed experimental setup, plus data-scaling ablations (Tab. 5).
Comprehensive related-work positioning and clear writing overall; code and dataset release promised.
weaknesses: Potential train-test leakage undermining the headline results: the benchmark's RAVEN and Sudoku subsets are generated from the exact same public pipelines (footnoted GitHub/Gitee links) as the PRS training data. The model's dramatic gains (RAVEN 14→95, Sudoku 0→60, accounting for most of the 20.9→43.7 average improvement) are likely in-distribution fitting rather than transfer. Excluding these two categories, the fine-tuned 7B model (~32 avg over six Bearer [REDACTED] does not clearly surpass Gemini-2.5-Pro (33.8) or even GPT-4o(cot) (23.9 across all; ~27 over Bearer [REDACTED], weakening the claim that perceptual supervision 'markedly enhances' MLLMs in general.

The benchmark is small: 1,000 questions total, with only 97–156 per Bearer [REDACTED] and ~100 per high-level category. Per-category differences of a few points are not statistically meaningful, and the benchmark may be saturable/overfittable quickly.

Single training run, single model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), single seed; no evidence the gains transfer to other architectures (e.g., InternVL) and no comparison to strong alternatives such as training on the same 80k samples without perceptual annotations (answer-only supervision) — this control is essential to isolate the value of the perceptual descriptions themselves.

Tab. 4 ablation is conducted on 'a subset of our synthetic dataset' with unspecified size, and feeding ground-truth structured perceptual descriptions as input is an oracle setting; the interpretation overstates what it shows about real-world perception deficits.

The manually collected civil-service data (translated from Chinese exams) carries contamination risk given that popular MLLM pretraining corpora likely include such widely circulated exam content; no decontamination analysis is reported.

Novelty is moderate: the perception-bottleneck diagnosis echoes prior findings (e.g., MathVerse, R1-OneVision's cross-modal formalization, MM-Eureka analyses), and the synthesis framework is a conventional rule-based renderer; the perceived-description-as-input experiment is a standard probing technique.

Presentation issues: apparent typo '770ok' samples (contradicts Table 1's total of 1000 for the benchmark), unclear relation between benchmark size and PRS output sizes in Tab. 2, sparse details on the human study protocol (how many subjects, per-category sampling), and Table 1/2/3 references are occasionally mismatched with the text.

strengths: The central claim—that fine-grained perception, rather than reasoning, is the primary bottleneck for MLLMs on abstract visual reasoning—is well-motivated and supported by the perceptual-description ablation (Tab. 4), which shows large accuracy gains when raw graphics are replaced with structured perceptual text.

Broad evaluation covering seventeen models, including eleven open-source and six proprietary systems with thinking modes and CoT prompting, providing a reasonably comprehensive snapshot of the current state of MLLMs on AVR.

The PRS synthesis framework is a sensible response to the scarcity of perceptually annotated AVR data, and the incremental-data ablation (Tab. 5) shows a clear monotonic trend supporting the utility of the generated supervision.

The benchmark construction pipeline (collection, cleaning, consolidation with twelve annotators and expert answer keys) is described with reasonable procedural detail, and answer-option distributions are reported.
weaknesses: Serious contamination/shortcut concern: the PRS training data is generated from the same rule categories and source material (Chinese civil service exam patterns; RAVEN and Sudoku generators following the same protocols) as the VisuRiddles test set. The near-perfect jump on RAVEN (14.0 → 95.0) and Sudoku (0.0 → 60.0) after fine-tuning strongly suggests the model memorizes the specific generator's rules and layouts rather than acquiring generalizable perceptual ability. There is no held-out rule split, no cross-rule generalization experiment, and no evaluation on any external AVR benchmark (e.g., PGM, I-RAVEN, ConceptARC) to demonstrate that gains transfer beyond the synthetic distribution.

The 'perception vs. reasoning' causal claim is overclaimed. The Tab. 4 ablation shows models perform better when the input is already a symbolic, structured description of the scene—effectively converting the task into symbolic reasoning. This demonstrates that textualized scene descriptions help, but it does not isolate 'perception' as the bottleneck; the synthetic rules are deliberately kept 'tractable', so the results say little about perception on hard real-world riddles.

Benchmark scale and composition are thin: only 1,000 questions, with several core categories at 69–117 samples (Other: 69, Attribute: 97), making per-category accuracy numbers noisy. Human baseline (63.0%) is reported without any details on the number of human raters, their protocol, or confidence intervals.

Evidence of overfitting to the synthetic distribution even in the paper's own numbers: the 'Other' category consistently degrades with training (23.9 → 21.3, -2.6), which the paper does not explain or address, undermining the claim of broad perceptual improvement.

Writing and presentation are sloppy: '770ok samples' (p.5), inconsistent category naming (Numerosity vs. Numerical vs. Quantitative across Sections 3.1, Fig. 2, and tables), a missing release URL in the abstract, 'Qwen2.5-8B' vs. 'PRS-Qwen2.5VL-7B' inconsistencies, duplicated citation [67], and a broken sentence at the end of Sec. 4.3.

Limited methodological novelty: benchmark-plus-synthetic-data-generation is a crowded design pattern; the synthesis itself (rule selection, element configuration, rendering with templated JSON annotations) is described only at a high level, with no quantitative analysis of distractor quality, rule-solvability checks, or annotation fidelity, hindering reproducibility.
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple-run results for the fine-tuning experiments, despite gains in Bearer [REDACTED] of only a few points (e.g., Numerosity 23.4 → 27.2).

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed research question: disentangling perceptual vs. reasoning failures in MLLMs on abstract visual reasoning, supported by a targeted ablation (Table 4) showing that substituting perceptual descriptions for raw images dramatically improves even strong closed-source models (e.g., GPT-4o avg +32.5), which is persuasive evidence for the perceptual bottleneck claim

The PRS synthesis framework is a useful contribution: it programmatically generates riddles aligned with structured perceptual annotations (layout metadata, element-level properties, reasoning traces), enabling supervision of intermediate perceptual stages rather than only final answers

Comprehensive evaluation across 17 models (11 open-source, 6 proprietary, including thinking-mode variants) with unified decoding via vLLM, plus a human baseline, giving a broad picture of the current state of AVR capability

Multi-stage dataset construction pipeline (collection from civil service exams, cleaning with 12 trained annotators, consolidation into standardized JSON) with reasonable quality control; balanced answer-option distributions suggest care against positional bias

Ablations on data scale (Table 5) show monotonic improvement with more perceptually annotated data, and the visualization/case-study analysis (Fig. 4) concretely illustrates the verbose-but-wrong behavior of thinking-mode vs. grounded reasoning of the fine-tuned model
weaknesses: Partial circularity / distributional overfitting concern: the headline gains of PRS-Qwen2.5VL-7B are concentrated on the Sudoku (0→60) and RAVEN (14→95) categories, which are generated from the same public codebases as the training data, so rule-space overlap between train and test is likely; meanwhile performance on the 'Other' category actually decreases (23.9→21.3), and gains on the human-collected civil-service categories are modest (e.g., Numerosity +3.8), which weakens the claim of a general perceptual capability improvement

The central causal claim ('fine-grained perception is the primary bottleneck') is only indirectly established: Table 4 uses oracle perceptual descriptions at inference time on a synthetic subset rather than the real benchmark, and the paper does not measure perception accuracy directly (e.g., via probing or perceptual-description generation accuracy) on VisuRiddles itself

Text/table inconsistencies raise reproducibility and quality-control concerns: '770ok samples' appears to be a typo and does not match Table 1 totals (800 Bearer [REDACTED] 200 high-level = 1000); the abstract's release URL is incomplete; Table 4 contains typos like '100.0(60.0)'

Fine-tuning is done only on Qwen2.5-VL-7B with a single training recipe; no results on other backbones, no comparison to alternative supervision strategies (e.g., training on answer-only synthetic data of the same scale, or RL-based methods), so the specific value of the perceptual annotations versus simply more in-domain synthetic data is not isolated

Benchmark scale is small (1000 questions, ~100-250 per category), some categories are quite small (Other: 69, Attribute: 97), human performance on Sudoku/RAVEN is not reported, and no statistical significance or variance analysis is provided

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the five-dimension taxonomy builds on existing cognitive literature, RAVEN/Sudoku components reuse existing generators, and training with perceptual/structural reformulations of visual inputs is similar in spirit to R1-OneVision's 'cross-modal formalization', which the paper cites but does not empirically compare against

strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: the paper targets abstract visual reasoning (AVR), an area where even frontier commercial models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3) score near random on the new benchmark, clearly establishing the problem's difficulty and relevance.

The central claim—that fine-grained perception, not reasoning capacity, is the primary bottleneck—is supported by a convincing ablation (Table 3): providing structured perceptual descriptions in place of raw images yields massive gains (e.g., Sudoku 0->65% for Qwen2.5VL-72B, +32.5 avg for GPT-4o), which is strong, direct evidence for the paper's thesis.

The VisuRiddles Synthesizer is a thoughtful design: programmatically generating instances with ground-truth perceptual descriptions, and using a commercial model to generate CoT only from descriptions (then filtering by answer correctness) is a pragmatic and clever way to obtain accurate reasoning traces despite current models' perceptual failures.

Broad and careful evaluation: 17 MLLMs including recent thinking-mode models, uniform decoding via vLLM, near-uniform answer distributions to mitigate format bias, human baselines, and an ablation table (Table 4) cleanly disentangling Caption/CoT/GRPO contributions (+8.7 vs +4.8 vs +14.9 over baseline).

Generalization is partially addressed: PAVR's gains transfer to the external VisuLogic benchmark (30.6 vs 26.0 for its 7B baseline), and qualitative case studies (Fig. 5) illustrate the 'rethink' behavior concretely.
weaknesses: Potential data contamination and provenance concerns: the benchmark is collected from the Chinese National Civil Service Examination with answers from the widely used Fenbi platform; such exam content is highly likely to appear in the pretraining corpora of the evaluated LLMs/MLLMs. The paper does not discuss or test for contamination, which weakens the benchmark's validity as a clean evaluation.

Training/evaluation circularity: the Synthesizer covers exactly the same seven reasoning categories, rule types, and layouts as the benchmark, and PAVR is trained on 24K synthetic instances from it. The large gains of PAVR-SFT/PAVR over zero-shot commercial models are therefore not an apples-to-apples comparison—part of the improvement may reflect fitting the synthetic rule distribution rather than general AVR ability. The cross-benchmark result on VisuLogic (30.6) actually falls slightly below InternVL2.5-38B-RL (31.1), suggesting the gains are partly benchmark-specific.

CoT supervision quality is only weakly controlled: reasoning traces from Gemini-2.5-Flash are validated solely by final-answer match; intermediate reasoning steps may still be wrong or spurious, and no human verification or quality analysis of the CoT data is provided.

Results are reported for a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); it is unclear how the method interacts with other base models or scales, and no comparison against strong recent AVR-focused training baselines (e.g., VisualSphinx-style synthetic RL) on VisuRiddles.

The benchmark is modest in scale (1000 samples; some categories only ~100, e.g., Sudoku/RAVEN with 100 each), making per-category results noisy, and human evaluation details (number of subjects, protocol) are sparse.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammar errors ('It unexpected that', 'claude-3-7-sonne(cot)', 'draw the following conclusions form the experiments'), an unfinished release URL in the abstract, and missing high-level results in the human row of Table 2 reduce polish.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored question: whether MLLMs fail at Abstract Visual Reasoning due to perception or reasoning, and provides a reasonably well-motivated decomposition of the problem.

The VisuRiddles benchmark is collected from real-world civil service exam riddles and covers eight reasoning categories with human baselines, offering a more realistic and challenging evaluation than purely synthetic benchmarks like RAVEN.

The evaluation is broad: ~25 models including strong commercial systems (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, o3, Claude-3.7-Thinking) are systematically compared, and the finding that scaling and CoT do not solve AVR is informative.

The ablations are reasonably complete: V-vs-P input experiments (Table 3) cleanly demonstrate the perception bottleneck, and Table 4 isolates the contributions of perceptual captions, CoT data, and GRPO.
Providing a synthesizer that produces structured perceptual descriptions and reasoning chains is a useful resource, and the overall paper is easy to follow with a coherent narrative.
weaknesses: Circularity / potential train-test contamination: the benchmark is drawn from Chinese civil service exams and the VisuRiddles Synthesizer explicitly 'extracts representative reasoning patterns from real-world standardized tests, such as civil service visual logic exams', with the same seven rule categories as the benchmark. The large PAVR gains (24.6 -> 46.8) may therefore largely reflect in-domain pattern familiarity rather than genuinely improved general perception. No train/test overlap analysis or out-of-domain distribution ablation is provided.

The out-of-domain result undercuts the central claim: on VisuLogic (Appendix D), PAVR achieves only 30.6 overall, which does not even beat InternVL2.5-38B-RL (31.1) despite being a 7B model trained specifically for this capability. This weakens the claim that fine-grained perception training provides a general solution to AVR.

The method itself has limited novelty: SFT on synthetic data followed by GRPO with answer/format rewards is now a standard recipe (e.g., R1-OneVision, Visual-Sphinx, MM-EUREKA), and the synthesizer closely resembles existing procedural generators such as RAVEN and VisualSphinx.
PAVR is developed and validated on only a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); there is no evidence the paradigm transfers across base models, which limits the generality of the conclusions.

The 'perceptual description input' results (Table 3, Fig. 1b) are somewhat oracle-like and could mislead: they show that removing perception entirely lets a text LLM succeed, but the resulting CoT annotations are generated by Gemini from the gold perceptual descriptions, meaning the SFT supervision is distilled from a model that never actually perceives the images; the reliability of this pipeline and its failure modes are not analyzed.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('It unexpected', 'a innovative', 'sonne(cot)', 'strength model's reasoning', 'form the experiments'), inconsistent notation and arithmetic formatting in Table 3 (e.g., '100.0(60.0)'), the code/dataset release URL in the abstract is empty, and Figure 3's cross-reference is malformed.

Human evaluation methodology is under-specified (how many subjects, what protocol, how Sudoku/RAVEN human performance was handled given '-' entries), and answer-option distributions and difficulty calibration for the exam-sourced items are only briefly described.

Several key details of the RL stage are thin: reward hacking analysis, training stability, and whether format rewards or answer rewards drive the gains are not disentangled, and GRPO is run for 40 epochs on only 4K instances without discussion of overfitting to the synthesized distribution.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies fine-grained perception as a bottleneck in abstract visual reasoning, and the design of the resource (benchmark + synthesizer + two-stage training) directly targets this claim.

The VisuRiddles benchmark is derived from real-world riddles (Chinese civil service exams) rather than purely synthetic sources, covers eight reasoning categories with defined evaluation dimensions, and includes a human baseline, making it a useful and challenging evaluation resource.
Comprehensive evaluation covering 17+ open-source and commercial MLLMs, including thinking-mode variants and CoT prompting, providing a broad snapshot of current MLLM capabilities on AVR.

The V vs. P ablation (Table 3) is a compelling experiment that directly supports the central claim: giving models structured perceptual descriptions yields very large gains (e.g., +42.7 avg for Qwen2.5-VL), isolating perception as a key failure mode.

The component ablation (Table 4) cleanly disentangles the contributions of perceptual SFT (Caption/CoT) and RL (GRPO), showing RL alone yields modest gains (+4.8) while perception-grounded SFT is essential (+14.9).

PAVR (7B) substantially outperforms much larger open-source and commercial models on VisuRiddles (46.8 vs. 33.9 for Gemini-2.5-Pro), and additional evaluation on the external VisuLogic benchmark provides some out-of-distribution evidence.

The synthesizer design (rule pool, perceptual descriptions in JSON, API labeling with answer-consistency validation) is reasonable and reproducible; construction pipeline details are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Potential train/test overlap inflates headline results: the benchmark's RAVEN and Sudoku subsets are generated from the same public generators and rule protocols as the VisuRiddles Synthesizer training data, and the synthesizer's rule pool was extracted from the same civil-service style patterns as the benchmark's core categories. The large PAVR gains on VisuRiddles (46.8) may therefore partly reflect distribution matching rather than genuine perceptual/reasoning improvements.

Out-of-distribution generalization is weak relative to the paper's claims: on VisuLogic, PAVR achieves only 30.6, below InternVL2.5-38B-RL (31.1) and only modestly above the 7B baseline (26.0), which undercuts the claim that PAVR 'substantially outperforms' other models beyond the authors' own benchmark.

The central 'perception is the primary bottleneck' claim rests heavily on the synthetic-subset ablation (Table 3); a similar perceptual-description experiment on the real riddle benchmark itself would strengthen the argument, since real riddles may involve ambiguity and knowledge that perceptual descriptions cannot resolve.
Benchmark scale is modest (1,000 samples; e.g., only 69 in 'Other') and there is no held-out test split with non-overlapping rules from the training distribution.

Data contamination and licensing concerns are not addressed: riddles from the civil service exam and the Fenbi platform likely circulate online and may appear in commercial model pretraining corpora; the paper does not discuss contamination checks or the copyright status of collected images/questions.
Human baseline is missing for the two high-level tasks (RAVEN, Sudoku) and human evaluation protocol (number of annotators, per-item agreement) is underspecified.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('It unexpected', 'a innovative', 'strength model's'), a typo in Table 2 ('claude-3-7-sonne(cot)'), and minor inconsistencies (e.g., Table 3 spatial delta formatting) reduce polish.
